description: Berber reform movement that crossed from North Africa (1147) to reunify Muslim Iberia under strict Maliki doctrine; at its peak ruled all of al-Andalus and the Maghreb, but defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) irreversibly broke Almohad power and opened Andalusia to Castilian reconquest.

temporal.notes: Defeated at Las Navas de Tolosa 1212; collapse follows

lifecycle_phases.description: Almohad forces from Morocco cross into Iberia, eliminate the taifa kingdoms and Almoravid remnants, and unify Muslim Iberia under a single puritanical Berber caliphate. Córdoba, Seville, and Granada fall to Almohad control.

Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur defeats Alfonso VIII at Alarcos (1195), inflicting the worst Christian defeat in the Reconquista. The defeat temporarily checks Christian expansion and forces the Christian kingdoms to form a coalition.

Coalition of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal crushes Almohad forces at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), a decisive turning point in the Reconquista. Internal Almohad succession crises and Berber tribal revolts shatter unity. Seville (1248) and other cities fall to Castile.

rise_factors.description: Almohad ('those who affirm divine unity') ideology offered a reformist Islamic challenge to both Almoravid perceived laxity and Christian expansion; puritanical religious zeal motivated military jihad and political consolidation

Almohad armies combined Berber tribal cavalry from Morocco with Iberian Muslim infantry; their unified command under the caliph solved the coordination problems that had doomed the fragmented taifa states

The Almohads (al-Muwahhidun = "those who affirm divine unity") launched a strict Maliki reform movement against Berber popular religion and Iberian Muslim laxity, mobilizing religious enthusiasm that sustained rapid conquest.

The Battle of Alarcos (1195) destroyed a Castilian army and forced Alfonso VIII to surrender dozens of fortresses. This victory demonstrated Almohad peak military power and temporarily halted the Reconquista.

Despite its religious intolerance, the Almohad period paradoxically stimulated philosophical and medical scholarship: Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides (both born in Córdoba) pursued their work partly in response to Almohad intellectual challenges.

The Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur's crushing victory at Alarcos (1195) over Alfonso VIII of Castile temporarily reversed Reconquista momentum and demonstrated the revitalized Islamic military capacity under Almohad discipline.

decline_factors.description: Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) broke Almohad military supremacy; the Christian coalition showed that Iberian kingdoms could coordinate effectively. Ferdinand III of Castile then conquered Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248) in rapid succession.
Almohad succession was disputed between family branches; the empire's North African base fragmented under Hafsid, Marinid, and Zayyanid challengers, removing support for the Iberian caliphate

The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), a combined Christian crusade force, shattered the Almohad army and opened Andalucia to rapid Christian conquest. Within 40 years, only Granada remained under Muslim rule.

Almohad authority rested on a Berber tribal confederation that proved fragile under military stress. Defeats triggered tribal secession; the Hafsids, Zayyanids, and Marinids all broke away as regional powers in the 1230s.
